output.methodChoice: Kepner-Tregoe-style specification (is/is-not) to localize, then competing-hypotheses weighing, with a source-stake check on the manager's and section lead's claims. Stopped without collecting more evidence.
output.brief:
The evidence points to one chance QC outlier, not a failing analyzer. Level 2 potassium was out by 3.8 SD once; the repeat from the same vial passed 21 minutes later. Levels 1 and 3, sodium and chloride were all fine. Across a month of QC there were no other rule violations, and every scheduled QC run was completed. That is about the one or two chance flags a month the QC plan expects. Re-testing 43 patient samples on Analyzer A agreed with Analyzer B within 0.02 mmol/L on average. The new reagent lot shows no shift, and the staffing-skipped-QC theory is contradicted by the QC log. Ward 6's high potassiums are split 7 and 7 between the two analyzers. They line up with slow sample transport since the tube station failed on 10 Nov, and with four renal overflow patients. That fits a pre-analytical cause, though it is not proven.

What to sign off: return Analyzer B potassium to service and close the review of the 186 flagged results with no amendments. Do not recall about 2,900 results, quarantine the lot, or widen the limits. Do not record a sampling glitch as the confirmed cause, because it cannot be shown. Tell Ward 6 the analyzers are not giving false highs. Ask them to repeat samples on the high results, and push to get the tube station fixed. An extra Level 2 QC at the start of each shift for a week is a reasonable precaution. Confidence is fairly high.
